extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of media, public opinion, journalism, and political theory; journalists and policy-makers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying principles about how news, censorship, communication channels, and social structures shape the formation and limits of public opinion. Useful for evaluating news production, propaganda tactics, and public-awareness campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Features of the world outside which have to do with the behavior of other human beings, in so far as that behavior crosses ours, is dependent upon us, or is interesting to us, we call roughly public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the elements that enter into public opinion — pictures in our heads about other people's behavior, their relations, and opinions. The passage stresses that public affairs are the subset of external reality that intersects with our interests and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on attention and time (need for compression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief factors limit their knowledge: the facts that are the arri v a l , relationships, habits, or social contacts, the comparative leisure time available in each group — messages have to be compressed into very short messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because public affairs must be compressed into short messages, complicated worlds and many facts are difficult to convey; this compression constrains what the public can know and understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures in our heads: role of stereotypes, stored images, prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: External messages are affected by stored images, prejudices which interpret, fill them out, and in their turn powerfully direct attention and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and communicators should recognize that audiences interpret news through pre-existing mental pictures; these stereotypes determine what is perceived and retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and privacy as barriers enabling propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Without some form of censorship, propaganda in the strict sense of the word is impossible. Access to the real environment must be limited before anyone can create a pseudo-environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Barriers (military censorship, legal powers, control of cables/passports, secrecy norms) allow authorities or groups to control what the public sees and thereby arrange news to suit purposes. Example: French military communiqués at Verdun were edited to steady the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of selection, framing and wording of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities can present only certain facts, and these only in such a way as would be most likely to steady the people — selecting words and phrases (e.g., inserting 'as had been anticipated') or omitting inconvenient facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing devices (choice of verbs, nouns, adjectives; omission or inclusion of particular items) create particular mental pictures and inferences without formal argument. Example: the French communiques omitted some truths and invented plausible battle plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics of information control (practical levers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Staff (or government) controls selection of correspondents, controls their movements at the front, reads and censors their messages, operates the wires, and the Government controls cables, passports, mails, custom houses, legal power over publishers, public meetings, and secret service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of concrete levers used to limit independent access and enforce censorship; also notes limits (enemy communiqués, soldiers' talk) that can leak information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of men, who can prevent independent access to the event, arrange the news of it to suit their purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stresses that propaganda requires the ability to restrict access and then to compose a pseudo-environment; the patriotic nature of the purpose does not change the mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for manufacturing belief (repetition, omission, emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated casualty figures and constant repetition (placing dead Germans in focus while omitting French dead) create a specific inference — e.g., that attrition favors the French — without an explicit argumentative case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how repetition and selective emphasis produce powerful impressions (the 'bloody background') and can neutralize other impressions (German territorial advances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy as an elastic barrier to public knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The frontier between what is concealed because publication is 'not compatible with the public interest' and what is 'none of the public's business' is elastic: incomes, salaries, directors' meetings, cabinet conversations, etc., are variously treated as private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding how social and legal norms about privacy restrict information is essential to assessing what reaches public opinion and why certain facts remain hidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and resource intensity required to reach 'everybody'
rubrics_metrics.description: To reach 'everybody' requires stupendous organization (example: Creel's wartime machinery — thousands of releases, tens of thousands of speakers, posters, slides, magazines sent to teachers, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: universal, uniform opinion requires vast personnel, money and logistics; in peacetime such mobilization rarely exists, so many groups remain uninformed or only vaguely aware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical, economic and institutional constraints on circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Means of communication (travel, trade, mails, wires, radio, railroads, highways, ships, aeroplanes) and their technical/economic/political conditions crucially affect the supply and quality of information: monopolies of cables/ports, costs, tariffs, and subsidies act as barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating news reach requires assessing infrastructure, monopoly controls, costs and regulation that limit or enable communication channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic status and access to the world outside
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's income and community income determine access: with money one can travel, buy books and periodicals, and overcome tangible obstacles of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socioeconomic disparities produce unequal information access; analysts should consider wealth as a determinant of exposure to news and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social set membership and normative gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Within social sets, opinions converge, are sorted out, and sanctioned; the set decides which authorities and sources of information are admissible. Social leaders act as custodians and interpreters of the set's pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public opinion is often locally bounded by social networks and accepted authorities; lateral imitation (Tarde's laws) and vertical imitation from powerful sets spread standards, but many populations lack cross-set channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-imposed limits on awareness (anemia of curiosity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large groups live in grooves, shut in among their own affairs, barred out of larger affairs, meet few people not of their own sort, read little — they are not limited by censorship but by lack of appetite and curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish structural barriers from voluntary isolation; remediation strategies differ (education, incentives, changing media offer) from those tackling censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical provenance test (ask how you got the facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often illuminating to ask how you got at the facts on which you base your opinion: who actually saw, heard, felt, counted, named the thing; how much was he permitted to see; what part of the country did he watch; what newspapers did he read?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This line of questioning fosters skepticism and serves as a protection against being misled by mediated or secondhand reports; recommended as an evaluative habit for consumers of news.
